ABSTRACT
Background: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are standard therapy for recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous 
cell carcinoma, but unleashing antitumour immunity can trigger immune-related adverse events (irAEs). Pneumothorax is a 
rare pulmonary complication compared with the more recognised ICI-associated pneumonitis.
Case report: A 67-year-old man with p16-positive, poorly differentiated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma presented 
with progressive bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and subsequently required tracheostomy and gastrostomy for upper-
airway obstruction. Chemoradiation with weekly docetaxel was discontinued early due to severe mucositis. Restaging 
showed regression of the primary tumour but new and enlarging subpleural pulmonary nodules consistent with metastases. 
Pembrolizumab was initiated. Within days of the first infusion, the patient developed pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. 
Upright chest radiography demonstrated a large right pneumothorax, and a computed tomography scan revealed bilateral 
subpleural lesions with adjacent parenchymal abnormalities; a contralateral pneumothorax was also present. Bilateral 
chest tubes were placed with symptomatic improvement. In the absence of trauma, mechanical ventilation, known bullous 
disease, or infectious cavitation, an immune-mediated mechanism was considered most likely: rapid necrosis and cavitation 
of subpleural metastases creating alveolar–pleural fistulas. Given poor functional reserve and advanced disease, definitive 
pleurodesis was deferred and palliative care was engaged.
Conclusion: Acute pneumothorax—sometimes bilateral—can occur shortly after PD-1 inhibition, particularly in patients 
with subpleural metastatic disease. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion when new respiratory symptoms 
arise soon after ICI initiation, obtain prompt imaging to distinguish pneumothorax from pneumonitis, and coordinate early 
multidisciplinary management to optimise outcomes and align treatment with patient goals.
KEYWORDS

INTRODUCTION
Immune-checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting PD-1/PD-L1 
have reshaped the management of recurrent/metastatic 
head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), conferring 
meaningful survival benefits[1]. By reinvigorating antitumour 
T-cell activity, however, ICIs can precipitate immune-related 
adverse events (irAEs) across multiple organs[2,3]. In the lung, 
pneumonitis is the prototypical irAE and a key diagnostic 
consideration when new respiratory symptoms arise after 
treatment initiation[4,5]. Spontaneous pneumothorax is far 
less common but increasingly recognised in association 
with ICIs[6–8]. We report a distinctive presentation of 
pembrolizumab-associated, 
bilateral 
pneumothoraces 
occurring within days of the first infusion in a man with 
p16-positive oropharyngeal carcinoma and subpleural 
pulmonary metastases. Salient features include the very 
early onset after cycle 1, bilateral involvement, absence 
of alternate precipitants (trauma, mechanical ventilation, 
bullous disease, or infection), and imaging that demonstrated 
subpleural lesions with adjacent parenchymal change—
collectively supporting a mechanism of rapid immune-
mediated tumour necrosis and cavitation with alveolar–
pleural fistula formation. Management required bilateral 
tube thoracostomy, while definitive pleurodesis was deferred 
in the context of limited physiological reserve and advanced 
disease. This case broadens the differential for early post-
ICI dyspnoea beyond pneumonitis and underscores the need 
for prompt imaging and multidisciplinary planning when 
subpleural metastases are present.
CASE DESCRIPTION
A 67-year-old man with p16-positive, poorly differentiated 
HPV associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma 
initially presented with progressive bilateral cervical 
lymphadenopathy. Rapid tumour enlargement precipitated 
upper-airway obstruction requiring tracheostomy and 
percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy. He underwent a 
7-week course of radiotherapy with concurrent weekly 
docetaxel, which was discontinued early because of severe 
mucositis. Post-treatment imaging demonstrated marked 
regression of the primary tumour and cervical nodes but 
new and enlarging pulmonary nodules consistent with 
metastatic disease. Pembrolizumab was commenced with 
palliative intent.

DISCUSSION
ICIs have improved survival in recurrent/metastatic HNSCC 
but introduce a spectrum of irAEs that frequently involve 
the lung parenchyma rather than the pleura[1–5]. Pneumonitis 
remains 
the 
prototypical 
pulmonary 
irAE; 
pleural 
complications are uncommon. Nevertheless, spontaneous 
pneumothorax has been increasingly described with PD-1/
PD-L1 blockade, particularly in patients with subpleural 
metastases[6–8].
Our case adds several distinctive features to this emerging 
literature. First, temporality: bilateral pneumothoraces 
occurred within days of the first pembrolizumab infusion, 
earlier than typically reported. Second, distribution: baseline 
imaging demonstrated subpleural metastatic deposits with 
interval parenchymal change contiguous with the pleural 
surface at the time of presentation. Third, exclusion of 
alternative precipitating factors: there was no trauma, 
positive-pressure ventilation, known bullous disease, or 
microbiological evidence of infection. Taken together, these 
elements support a systemic immune mechanism rather 
than mechanical or infectious aetiologies.
Several pathophysiological pathways may underlie ICI-
associated pneumothorax. The leading hypothesis—well 
aligned with our patient’s clinicoradiological course—is 
immune-mediated necrosis and cavitation of subpleural 
metastases resulting in alveolar–pleural fistulae[6–8]. An 
alternative is parenchymal destruction secondary to ICI 
pneumonitis, whereby diffuse or focal inflammatory injury 
culminates in alveolar rupture and air leak[4,5]. In this case, 
the very early onset after cycle-1 pembrolizumab, bilateral 
involvement, and subpleural tumour geography most 
strongly favour the first mechanism.
This presentation carries important diagnostic implications. 
Early post-ICI dyspnoea and pleuritic pain are commonly 
attributed to pneumonitis; however, pneumothorax should 
be co-prioritised in the differential, especially when baseline 
imaging reveals subpleural disease. A low threshold for 
immediate chest radiography is warranted, with chest 
CT scan to define the extent of pneumothorax, identify 
fistulous tracts or cavitation, and characterise concomitant 
parenchymal irAEs. Prompt recognition is critical given the 
risk of rapid deterioration, including tension physiology.
Management should follow contemporary guidelines for 
spontaneous pneumothorax, recognising that most ICI-
associated events in patients with underlying metastatic lung 
involvement meet criteria for secondary pneumothorax and 
often require tube thoracostomy rather than observation 
alone[9]. In our patient, bilateral tube thoracostomy 
produced rapid symptomatic improvement and radiographic 
re-expansion. Decisions regarding definitive pleurodesis 
or surgical intervention must balance recurrence risk 
(heightened with persistent subpleural disease) against 
performance status, anticipated cancer trajectory, and the 
patient’s goals of care[9]. Multidisciplinary coordination 
among oncology, pulmonology, thoracic surgery, and 
palliative care is therefore essential.
From a preventive and counselling standpoint, clinicians 
should (i) review pre-ICI imaging for subpleural metastases 
as a potential risk marker, (ii) educate patients to report 
new chest pain or dyspnoea immediately after treatment 
initiation, and (iii) maintain expedited access to imaging and 
intervention. While these data do not justify withholding 
effective immunotherapy, they argue for heightened 
vigilance in anatomically high-risk settings.
Limitations include the absence of histopathological 
confirmation and the possibility that occult pneumonitis-
mediated alveolar rupture contributed to the air leak. 
Prior radiotherapy and chemotherapy may also modulate 
tissue fragility. Even so, the temporal relationship, anatomic 
concordance with subpleural lesions, and lack of alternative 
precipitants make an ICI-triggered mechanism the most 
plausible explanation.

Abstract: Background: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are standard therapy for recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, but unleashing antitumour immunity can trigger immune-related adverse events (irAEs). Pneumothorax is a rare pulmonary complication compared with the more recognised ICI-associated pneumonitis. Case report: A 67-year-old man with p16-positive, poorly differentiated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma presented with progressive bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and subsequently required tracheostomy and gastrostomy for upper- airway obstruction. Chemoradiation with weekly docetaxel was discontinued early due to severe mucositis. Restaging showed regression of the primary tumour but new and enlarging subpleural pulmonary nodules consistent with metastases. Pembrolizumab was initiated. Within days of the first infusion, the patient developed pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. Upright chest radiography demonstrated a large right pneumothorax, and a computed tomography scan revealed bilateral subpleural lesions with adjacent parenchymal abnormalities; a contralateral pneumothorax was also present. Bilateral chest tubes were placed with symptomatic improvement. In the absence of trauma, mechanical ventilation, known bullous disease, or infectious cavitation, an immune-mediated mechanism was considered most likely: rapid necrosis and cavitation of subpleural metastases creating alveolar–pleural fistulas. Given poor functional reserve and advanced disease, definitive pleurodesis was deferred and palliative care was engaged. Conclusion: Acute pneumothorax—sometimes bilateral—can occur shortly after PD-1 inhibition, particularly in patients with subpleural metastatic disease. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion when new respiratory symptoms arise soon after ICI initiation, obtain prompt imaging to distinguish pneumothorax from pneumonitis, and coordinate early multidisciplinary management to optimise outcomes and align treatment with patient goals.
